   <shape width=\"145.3\" height=\"12\" topLeftX=\"387.6\" topLeftY=\"322.3\" type=\"text\" id=\"bdZ\">\n        <content fontSize=\"12\" fontFamily=\"思源黑体\" color=\"rgba(148, 163, 184, 1)\" textAlign=\"left\" wrap=\"false\" defaultTabSize=\"47.0047\">\n          <p>sharper with every run</p>\n        </content>\n      </shape>\n    </data>\n    <note id=\"bhH\">\n      <content>\n        <p>This is the heart of the product. We do not produce a single forecast and walk away. We run a closed loop: the living world simulates forward, we intervene with a decision or a rumor, we observe how the crowd reacts, we turn that into a probability forecast, and the decision-maker acts. Acting changes the world, which feeds the next simulation. Because every run is compared against what actually happened, the engine gets more calibrated over time.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pkf\">\n    <style>\n      <fill produces four distinct outputs. First, opinion and sentiment: we track grievance, legitimacy and mood for every resident. Second, scenario simulation: we replay a decision or a rumor inside a living world that can be checked. Third, probabilistic forecasting: we return P10 to P90 outcomes calibrated against historical cases. Fourth, decision support: we compare options, test sensitivity, and let the decision-maker act. These are not four separate products; they are four reads of one simulated world.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJk\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJk\">\n </shape>\n    </data>\n    <note id=\"bdt\">\n      <content>\n        <p>Pure neural world models hallucinate and cannot be checked; pure symbolic engines are rigid. We combine them. At the bottom is L1, symbolic truth: a typed World Spec, a deterministic simulator, and versioned WorldOps that can be rolled back. Above it sits the living society of residents. L2 is a small neural layer that imagines consequences and can only advise, never overwrite L1. L3 is the render layer, a playable skin. If the video breaks, the 2D game still runs because L1 keeps the world consistent. This is why our worlds are both generative and checkable.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJJ\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJJ\">\n        <fillColor    <p>Video world models give you pixels you cannot verify. Our world is a typed specification, validated by schema, with one source of truth. The simulator is deterministic: the same inputs always produce the same world, so a result can be reproduced. Every change is a typed WorldOp that records its parent, forming a revision lineage. You can inspect why a resident did something and roll back to any earlier state. A world that can be checked and replayed is trustworthy in a way that a generated video never is. That is the first layer of the moat.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJr\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJr\">\n        <fillColor color=\"rgba(10, 14, 20, 1)\"/>\n We prevent both. A natural-language prompt is first compiled into a typed intent, then into a promise contract: the genre, the place, the jobs, and the population the author commits to. The world is generated against that contract, and a gate checks every promise before release. If a promise is missing, the system regenerates instead of shipping a template. What the author promises is what the world demonstrably contains. living agent: they hold memory, keep a daily plan, have four needs that can interrupt that plan, and run opinion dynamics that become grievance, legitimacy, and rumors. The key addition is an inner world model running inside every heartbeat. A resident predicts where the crowd will be next, then compares that with what actually happens. The gap is surprise, which raises curiosity and drives the resident to walk over and look. Because attention is earned by surprise rather than scripted, behavior is genuinely emergent; a gate guards the emergence and a template is the fallback. This is a society that lives on its own.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJl\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJl\">\n        <fillColor color=\"rgba(10, 14, 20, single guess. The engine runs a Monte Carlo ensemble of futures, seeded from two presets: a contested decision and an exercise near a residential area. Each run is a complete simulation, and the ensemble becomes a probability distribution: P10, P50, and P90 bands for turnout, casualties, hotspots, and the escalation timeline, together with the causal chain, alternatives, and a sensitivity analysis. Crucially, those probabilities are calibrated against a library of historical cases, using a Brier score, case distance, and interval coverage. That means the number we call 80 percent actually happens about 80 percent of the time. This is a forecast you can trust and audit, not a confident hallucination.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJU\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJU\">\n </shape>\n    </data>\n    <note id=\"bFe\">\n      <content>\n        <p>Before acting in the real world, a decision-maker can run every option: hold, de-escalate, or deter. Each intervention is simulated as a full ensemble, so the decision-maker sees not just a predicted outcome but the probability band around it, the casualties and turnout implied, and the risk of a sudden spike. In this illustrative comparison, opening dialogue lowers the median escalation while holding leaves it high; deterrence can work but carries a tail risk. A sensitivity analysis then shows which assumptions, such as crowd size or rumor speed, move the result most. The system does not make the decision, but it makes the trade-offs visible and comparable before anyone commits.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJe\">\n    <style>\n <content>\n        <p>There is one world, but it presents two surfaces. To an observer or a forecaster it is an object to watch, simulate, and place predictions on. To a player, that same world is a game to enter and alter. Both sit on the identical checkable, living core, so a player&apos;s action and a forecaster&apos;s prediction are about the same evolving reality. This is why the product is not a game and not a forecasting tool: it is a world that supports both. The architecture also degrades gracefully: if the 3D or video layer fails, the 2D game stays playable, and the world itself keeps running. One world, two ways in, no single point of failure.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJt\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJt\">\n        <fillColor color=\"rgba(10, 14, On the world track, watching is free and the product is the prediction: users place bets, and the platform takes a 15 percent rake, most of which goes to the author. On the game track, playing is free and the product is drama cards: small, reversible in-world enhancements, with 70 percent to the author and a half-price first card to pull new players in. On the cost side, authors pay to activate their world, lighting it for today or this week, while the platform never charges a visitor per visit. This aligns everyone: authors earn from both tracks, visitors pay only for the moments they choose, and the platform is paid for outcomes rather than access.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n     <p>One-sided, silent, stopped, or tied: full refund</p>\n        </content>\n      </shape>\n    </data>\n    <note id=\"baB\">\n      <content>\n        <p>Each world runs one market, seeded automatically. The lock point is set at 12, 24, or 48 hours. The market opens, closes four hours later, and then spends four hours gathering evidence. The verdict comes from the town&apos;s real dialogue and living evidence, not from the author, who cannot change the result and cannot bet on their own market. A market forms only when both sides have stakes. The platform takes 15 percent, 70 percent of that goes to the author, and winners split the rest, with an 8x cap per bet. If the market is one-sided, silent, the clock stops, or the result is tied, every stake is refunded. The rules are designed to be fair and self-policing, which is what makes strangers willing to bet.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJx\">\n    <style>\n      <fill    </content>\n      </shape>\n    </data>\n    <note id=\"bac\">\n      <content>\n        <p>Most generated content is consumed once and never revisited. A living world is different because it does not pause when the user leaves. Residents keep living, opinions keep moving, and the clock on any open prediction keeps running. That gives three concrete reasons to return: a prediction that is still open and waiting to settle, a world that has visibly changed overnight, and a personal story that is still in motion. We reinforce the habit on the game track with a multiplier for same-day returning players. Retention here is not a notification strategy; it is a structural consequence of a world that genuinely continues. The product has a tomorrow, which is the first thing a recurring-revenue business needs.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJq\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJq\">\n        <fillColor color=\"rgba(10, 14, 20, 1)\"/>\n      </fill>\n    </style>\n    <data>\n      <shape width=\"500\" height=\"20\" topLeftX=\"56\" topLeftY=\"42\" type=\"text\" id=\"byP\">\n        <content textType=\"caption\" fontSize=\"12\" fontFamily=\"Inter\" color=\"rgba(34, 211, 238, 1)\" bold=\"true\" letterSpacing=\"3\" wrap=\"false\">\n          <p>09 · COMPETITION</p>\n        </content>\n      </shape>\n      <shape width=\"848\" height=\"48\" topLeftX=\"56\" topLeftY=\"70\" type=\"text\" id=\"byG\">\n        <content textType=\"title\" fontSize=\"34\" fontFamily=\"Montserrat\" color=\"rgba(241, 245, 249, 1)\" bold=\"true\" wrap=\"false\">\n          <p>Competitive landscape</p>\n        </content>\n      </shape>\n      <shape width=\"848\" height=\"24\" topLeftX=\"56\" topLeftY=\"118\" type=\"text\" id=\"byF\">\n        <content fontSize=\"14\" fontFamily=\"Inter\" color=\"rgba(148, 163, 184, 1)\" wrap=\"false\">\n          <p>Others build one layer. Chat-to-code tools generate code, but they have no checkable world, no continuous society, and no market. Video world models produce impressive clips, but they are not truly playable or auditable. The NPC-town research pioneered living agents, but those demos are not playable, not checkable, and not monetized. OpenGame is the only system that combines all five: a playable surface, a checkable world, continuous living evolution, opinion and rumor dynamics, and a prediction market on top. The moat is not any single feature; it is the combination, because each layer makes the others more valuable. A competitor would have to build all five at once, and they are already integrated and running.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJF\">\n    <style>\n      <fill It outputs probabilities, not certainties, and a genuinely unprecedented event cannot be forecast; we show the bands and keep the tails open. The quality of a prediction depends on the quality of the world spec, which is why specs are typed and the simulator is deterministic. Calibration is only as good as the case library, and we are growing it while disclosing how close the nearest case is. On edge cases, generation can still fail, so gates and a template fallback protect the output and a human reviews. The system is a decision aid that makes trade-offs visible, not a replacement for judgment. We believe this honesty is itself a reason to trust the numbers.</p>\n      </content>\n    </note>\n  </slide>\n  <slide id=\"pJR\">\n    <style>\n      <fill id=\"fJR\">\n        <fillColor
